items.text: In observation. <break time="0.8s" /> The best plan is obviously to decide beforehand. <break time="0.8s" /> Exactly what needs to be observed. <break time="0.8s" /> And then to focus attention. <break time="0.8s" /> On this precise point. <break time="0.8s" /> Reading may be called a kind of observation. <break time="0.8s" /> Since the reader is looking for. <break time="0.8s" /> What the author has to tell. <break time="0.8s" /> And the rule that holds for other observations. <break time="0.8s" /> Holds also for reading. <break time="0.8s" /> That is to say. <break time="0.8s" /> That the reader finds the most. <break time="0.8s" /> When he knows just what he is looking for. <break time="0.8s" /> We can learn something here from story reading. <break time="0.8s" /> Which is the most efficient sort of reading. <break time="0.8s" /> In the sense that you get the point of the story. <break time="0.8s" /> Better than that of more serious reading matter. <break time="0.8s" /> The reason being that attention is always pressing forward. <break time="0.8s" /> In the story. <break time="0.8s" /> Looking for something very definite. <break time="0.8s" /> You want to know. <break time="0.8s" /> How the hero gets out of the fix he is in. <break time="0.8s" /> And you press forward and find out. <break time="0.8s" /> With great certainty and little loss of time. <break time="0.8s" /> The best readers of serious matter. <break time="0.8s" /> Have a similar eagerness. <break time="0.8s" /> To discover what the author has to say. <break time="0.8s" /> They get the authors question. <break time="0.8s" /> And press on to find his answer. <break time="0.8s" /> Such readers are both quick and retentive.
